name: Dark Naphthalene Violet
lede: Dark Naphthalene Violet darkens [[naphthalene-violet]], a hue Robert Ridgway plotted on plate XXXVII of his 1912 color atlas, and the darkened form was itself picked up as its own named block in the 1955 ISCC-NBS dictionary.

sections.title: A Ridgway hue, darkened
sections.body:
The name pairs the modifier dark with [[naphthalene-violet]], one of the dye-derived violet hues Ridgway charted in *Color Standards and Color Nomenclature* (1912), plate XXXVII, hue 61′′, tone m [1]. Naphthalene violet itself is named for a coal-tar (naphthalene) dye family, part of the wave of synthetic colorants that followed mauveine [1].

Unlike most of our dark-modifier names, this darkened tone was filed in its own right: the ISCC-NBS *Dictionary of Color Names* carried it forward in 1955 as block 229 [1]. Its nearest measured neighbor is [[dark-umber]], 4.3 units off and redder; [[plum-grey]] and [[anthracene-purple]] sit about as close, both lighter and redder [2].

sections.title: Field notes
sections.body: A match for this color covers at least five per cent of a canvas in 182 of 23,781 paintings in our archive, about 0.8 per cent, as photographed [3]. Edvard Munch's work carries it almost eight times the archive's average rate, in 3 of his 50 paintings, and the 1900s overall run at 3.4 times the archive rate [3]. The earliest dated match is a *Jingoji Sutra and Wrapper*, 1099, a floor on the color's age in painting rather than a claim of its first appearance [3]. As photographed: these are computed color matches on museum photographs of aged, varnished paintings, not a pigment test [3].
